name: Thymosin alpha-1
lead: Thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1) is a 28-amino-acid peptide, N-terminally acetylated, produced by cleavage of a longer precursor called prothymosin alpha. It was the first peptide from the calf-thymus preparation known as thymosin fraction 5 to be completely sequenced and synthesised [1]. Its synthetic form is known as thymalfasin and has been sold under the brand name Zadaxin; Wikipedia states it is approved in some countries for hepatitis B and C and is used to boost immune responses in other diseases [1].

Unlike most compounds on this wiki, thymosin alpha-1 has a substantial human research record, but that record concerns medical conditions such as chronic viral hepatitis, sepsis, severe infections, pancreatitis and cancer adjunct care, not appearance [2][3][14]. In biohacking and longevity discussions it is described as an 'immune optimiser' and is mentioned in peptide stacks, usually by people who already use other peptides and hormones [17][18][19].

The 2001 pharmacology review covered its adverse effects in clinical trials. No published study was identified that tests thymosin alpha-1 for cosmetic or physique outcomes in healthy people. A 2025 review argues that its immune effects might be relevant to age-related immune decline, and states that further research is needed to validate long-term efficacy and safety in older people [4].
infobox: Approved in some countries for hepatitis B/C (not by the US FDA per Grokipedia) [1][5]

paras: Thymosin alpha-1 is derived from a precursor of about 113 amino acids, prothymosin alpha, encoded by the PTMA gene, and has the sequence Ac-SDAAVDTSSEITTKDLKEKKEVEEEAEN according to Wikipedia. It is genetically and chemically unrelated to the beta thymosins [1]. A structural review describes the thymosin proteins as short, highly charged and intrinsically unstructured under natural conditions [7].

Reviews describe the thymosins as a family of peptides with diverse functions rather than true thymic hormones; a 2007 review notes that none of the peptides isolated from fraction 5 turned out to be a bona fide thymic hormone [8].

Wikipedia reports approval in some countries for hepatitis B and C, with use as an immune-boosting adjunct in other diseases; it is given by subcutaneous injection [1]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, states that Zadaxin has been approved in more than 35 countries mainly in Asia, Latin America, Eastern Europe and the Middle East, has not received FDA approval in the United States, and was licensed commercially by SciClone Pharmaceuticals [5]. These regulatory details are unverified here.

A 1984 review summarised the early programme, noting that thymosin fraction 5 had corrected immune deficiencies in animal models and some patients, and that several component peptides had been purified [9].

subs.h: Use in appearance and longevity communities
paras: Forum posts describe thymosin alpha-1 as part of 'anti-inflammatory' peptide protocols alongside thymosin beta-4 and BPC-157, as a suggestion for a spouse with health problems, and as a suggested option for post-COVID fatigue [17][18][19][20]. It is not marketed for looks, and its connection to appearance is indirect, through ideas about immune health and ageing.

Wikipedia states that thymosin alpha-1 is an agonist of toll-like receptors 2 and 9 on myeloid and dendritic cells, stimulating adaptive immunity [1]. A 2004 study in Blood reported that Tα1 induced functional maturation and IL-12 production in dendritic cells exposed to Aspergillus fumigatus through TLR signalling [6]. An older pharmacology review described its action as augmenting T-cell function, possibly by stimulating thymocyte differentiation [2]. A 2025 review characterises it as immunomodulatory, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant, and says it can improve vaccine response in older people in preclinical and clinical studies [4].

A 2001 pharmacology review reported that Tα1 is rapidly absorbed after subcutaneous administration, reaches peak serum concentration within two hours, returns to baseline within 24 hours, and has a serum half-life of about two hours [2].

In chronic hepatitis B, the 2001 review summarised four clinical trials in 195 patients. One found HBV DNA clearance at six months in 9 of 17 patients on Tα1 versus 10 of 16 on interferon alfa-2b and 4 of 15 historical controls; an open-label trial reported 53 percent clearance; and a randomised trial reported 40.6 and 25.6 percent clearance for 6 and 12 months of treatment [2]. Later randomised trials were run in Japan [10][11], and a 2015 editorial discussed Tα1 treatment in chronic hepatitis B [12].

In critical illness, a multicentre randomised trial in China, the ETASS trial, tested Tα1 in severe sepsis [13]. A multicentre double-blind randomised trial tested early Tα1 in patients with predicted severe acute necrotising pancreatitis to see whether it reduces infected pancreatic necrosis [14], with a post hoc analysis in patients with metabolic abnormalities published in 2024 [15]. Wikipedia states that trials suggest it may be useful in septic shock, acute respiratory distress syndrome, pancreatitis and several infections, and that it has been studied alongside chemotherapy in cancer [1].

For COVID-19, a 2020 observational study reported that Tα1 was associated with lower mortality in severe disease through restoration of lymphocyte counts [16]. Wikipedia notes that two 2023 reviews reached differing conclusions on hospitalised patients, one finding no mortality or length-of-stay benefit and another finding reduced mortality but not length of stay [1].
A 2023 review addresses Tα1 in cancer immunoregulation [21].

Human research is extensive for medical indications. Randomised trials in chronic hepatitis B [2][10][11], severe sepsis [13] and acute necrotising pancreatitis [14][15] are summarised above, with observational data in COVID-19 [16] and ongoing work in older adults and cancer. Registered trials include a completed sepsis trial in 366 patients (NCT00711620) [22], a phase 3 sepsis trial in 1,106 patients (NCT02867267) [23], a phase 4 pancreatitis trial in 508 patients (NCT02473406) [24], a phase 2 melanoma trial combining Tα1 and interferon with dacarbazine in 488 patients (NCT00911443) [25], a phase 3 adjuvant colorectal cancer trial planned for 2,500 patients and listed as recruiting (NCT05086614) [26], and a phase 1 trial of Tα1 as an enhancer of COVID-19 booster response in older adults (NCT06821100) [27].
No studies were found of thymosin alpha-1 for cosmetic, physique or recovery outcomes in healthy people.

The 2001 pharmacology review covered adverse effects and dosage alongside efficacy and described the drug in phase II and III trials at that time [2]. Immune stimulation is a theoretical concern in autoimmune disease or transplantation, and no systematic safety data for use by healthy people were identified in the sources reviewed. Products obtained outside regulated channels may differ in quality, a general concern with unregulated peptides rather than a finding specific to thymosin alpha-1.

Research on the thymus and immunity grew from early observations that removal of the thymus produced immune deficiency. Grokipedia attributes the isolation of Tα1 from thymosin fraction 5 to Allan Goldstein and colleagues in 1977 [5]; Wikipedia notes it was the first of the fraction 5 peptides to be fully sequenced and synthesised [1]. The 1984 review documents the thymosin work at that point [9]. Prothymosin alpha, the precursor of Tα1, was isolated from rat thymus in 1984 [28].

Clinical development in hepatitis B in the 1980s and 1990s and approvals in a number of countries followed; Grokipedia reports patents on synthetic production methods and licensing to SciClone Pharmaceuticals [5]. In the 2000s and 2010s Tα1 was tested in sepsis and in cancer adjunct settings [13][25], and in 2020 it was investigated in COVID-19 [16].

Current work includes large phase 3 oncology trials [26], vaccine-response studies in older adults [27] and fusion drugs such as Refnot, which a 2025 review describes as combining Tα1 immunomodulation with the antitumour activity of TNF-alpha at reduced toxicity [4].

lore.intro: Thymosin alpha-1 is a minor topic on bodybuilding forums such as T Nation, where it appears in lists of peptides used for immunity and recovery. [17][18][19][20]

claims.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 optimises or boosts the immune system in healthy people.
claims.believers: Posters recommend it for fatigue after COVID or for family members, and include it in anti-inflammatory peptide protocols [17][19][20].
claims.experts: Human trials concern patients with hepatitis B, sepsis, pancreatitis or cancer, not healthy people; a 2025 review says more research is needed to confirm long-term efficacy and safety in older adults [2][4][13].

claims.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 helps with chronic viral infections such as hepatitis B.
claims.believers: Community posts treat it as an established immune-modulating peptide.
claims.experts: Trials in hepatitis B reported viral clearance in some patients, with results varying by trial and comparator, and it is approved in some countries for hepatitis B and C [1][2][10][12].

claims.claim: It reduces mortality in severe infections such as sepsis or COVID-19.
claims.believers: Users citing the COVID literature recommend it for post-infection fatigue [20].
claims.experts: Sepsis and pancreatitis have been tested in randomised trials [13][14]; for COVID-19 an observational study reported lower mortality [16], while Wikipedia notes that two 2023 reviews conflicted [1].

claims.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 improves appearance or slows visible ageing.
claims.believers: Appearance claims appear mostly indirectly, through general anti-ageing and immune optimisation ideas.
claims.experts: No published study tests Tα1 for skin, hair or physique outcomes; a 2025 review addresses immune ageing, not cosmetic ageing [4].
